item.title: Passportless mess
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
A fool, a genius, or ‘a man who destroys everything’? Piecing together Zoran, a mythic figure of Belgrade

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
‘He is, in simple terms, a man who destroys everything.’

In this entertaining short documentary from the Czech filmmaker Maja Penčič, truth and myth collide in the figure of Zoran, a former resident of a block of flats in Belgrade, Serbia, whose larger-than-life personality and convoluted biography have left behind accounts that can’t be reconciled. Penčič sets out to find Zoran, or at least to understand who he was, by surveying the people who claim to have known him at different stages of his life. Throughout, a rotating cast of acquaintances characterise him as everything from ‘warm’, ‘intelligent’ and ‘exceptional’ to someone who ‘never feels shame’ to, quite simply, ‘a dick’. The home-video aesthetic lends the proceedings an intimacy and a faintly surreal quality that evokes the imperfections of memory. The film never settles on a single version of events, instead watching the details rearrange themselves around a few fixed points, until what is left is less a man than a cautionary tale.

item.title: Don’t use the ‘C-word’
item.dc:creator: Matthew R Cooperberg
item.description:
A cancer diagnosis carries with it fear and upheaval. For many patients the cellular changes do not warrant the label

- by Matthew R Cooperberg

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

30 minute listen

William came to me for a third opinion. He was 53 and healthy, with a wife and two teenage children, a busy job, and a typically hectic work-and-family schedule. He’d taken time to do the right thing and had visited his primary care provider for a routine health exam and blood tests, his first in many years. A few weeks later, he’d found himself in an unfamiliar urologist’s office, at the edge of an abyss, ears ringing with what may be three of the most dreaded words in medicine: ‘You have cancer.’ This diagnosis portends pain, suffering and death: in the United States alone, cancer kills more than 600,000 people a year, enough lives to empty a city.

Yet, receiving a cancer diagnosis doesn’t necessarily mean what it once did. William was in very broad company: more than 2 million Americans a year receive the diagnosis and, for many, the finding entails little to no threat to length or quality of life, except through the ill effects of treatments. However, patients labelled with the ‘C-word’ face substantial clinical, psychological, social and economic consequences. This disconnect – between what the word evokes in my exam room and what it often describes in contemporary practice – drives controversies and variability in screening practices, and in light of our growing understanding of cellular biology, demands that we rethink what we really mean when we apply the label ‘cancer’.

William’s cancer was in his prostate, an organ of whose existence he was previously only vaguely aware, but whose removal or radiation risked impairments to urinary, bowel and sexual function. His biopsy had revealed a prostate tumour we designate ‘grade group 1’, which features few molecular hallmarks of cancer and no immediate potential for metastasis or death. Nonetheless, beset with many competing opinions from his rapidly expanding medical team, William found himself rushing headlong toward treatment, and wrestling with a constant anxiety he’d never felt before. By the time he reached my office, he had taken medical leave from work and confided that, perversely, he was smoking for the first time in decades.

When I started medical school in the 1990s, I found cancer fascinating and terrifying exactly because of the betrayal it represented. Most human disease represents failure of one body system or another. Whether due to trauma, infection, degradation of blood supply, mechanical wear-and-tear or other causes, one or more organs stop performing optimally. In such cases, our job in medicine is simple in principle: support the failing system, prevent further damage, and repair or replace missing function as much as possible.

Cancer is fundamentally different: although ultimately it also causes system failures, its origin lies in cells in a corner of a given organ thriving more than they should, growing too quickly, and eventually exploring and colonising other parts of the body. A marauding virus or bacterium is clearly a malign invader that can be understood and labelled as foreign and hostile. A cancer is a person’s own cells. They are behaving badly but are still intrinsic to the self. Chemotherapy for cancer is so much more toxic than antibiotics for bacterial infection precisely because it is harder for treatments to consistently distinguish ‘normal’ from ‘cancer’ among a body’s cells.

The noun, the proper noun with the capital letter, still looms, menacing

In my practices at the University of California, San Francisco Cancer Center and the San Francisco Veterans Affairs Medical Center, I see men in William’s situation in every clinic, every week. The better-informed among them have often already figured out that not every tumour needs treatment, but many are still reeling from the moment the word ‘cancer’ entered the room – the way the light suddenly dimmed and the air thickened – and how little they really heard during the rest of the visit. Counselling these patients is as important and nuanced a part of my job as is surgery, and the right words in the office are no less critical than the right tools in the operating room. But even as we have developed robot-assisted precision surgical systems, increasingly focused radiation delivery platforms and marvellously targeted pharmaceuticals, our language is essentially stuck in the 19th century.

Many colleagues and I try to pepper these counselling conversations with adjectives intended to reassure both patients and their loved ones: low-grade, low-risk, nonthreatening, slow-growing, indolent. We’ve grown relatively facile using these modifiers to pull patients back from the edge of the chasm, but the noun, the proper noun with the capital letter, still looms, menacing. After many years of these patient consultations – which have grown easier over time, but only to an extent – I am among a growing cadre of prostate cancer specialists and researchers who have started to challenge our colleagues to take seriously the question of whether to update our vocabulary to bring what we say back in line with what patients hear.

My professional forebears would recognise cancer at human scale quickly and with a knowing dread: the lump in the breast accompanied by another in the armpit, the yellowed eyes indicating a squeezed bile duct, the minor bleeding that wouldn’t stop because leukaemia had taken over the bone marrow. The unintended weight loss. The nagging pain. In my time, in contrast, we typically present a patient with the diagnosis over a piece of paper or text on a computer screen: a pathology report, a divination read from glass slides and rendered in ink or pixels to predict the future for a patient who today usually feels just fine. But at what point does aberrant behaviour threaten the whole body? How do we determine the thresholds cells cross from variant to abnormality to enemy? In the decades of my career since school, our appreciation of cancer’s complexity has grown more sophisticated, but we are still nowhere near being able to define the true moment a cancer begins, nor the subsequent moment it first threatens health and life.

Medical traditions stretching over thousands of years recognised visible growths with the capa­city to grow, spread and kill. Hippocrates and his contemporaries in the 5th century BCE first named the karkinos – ‘the crab’ – after the visible tendrils that progressive tumours could be seen to propagate along lymphatic channels under the skin. In the ensuing millennia, progress in understanding the disease came in fits and starts, but cancers were universally detected when they were visible, palpable or symptomatic, by which point cure with surgery was successful only uncommonly. Even when survivable in the hard-to-imagine pre-anaesthesia, pre-antisepsis era, surgery couldn’t eradicate cancer that had already metastasised; as a result, cancers recurred and progressed – and were nearly always lethal.

In the centuries after the development of microscopy, modern pathology evolved to allow researchers and physicians to see the hidden face of the adversary: the minute cells devolved from their proper roles in the broader organism and hellbent on reproduction and migration. By the late 19th century, improved microscopes allowed early pathologists to categorise cancers – carcinomas – based not just on their organs of origin but also on the appearance of the cells themselves, laying the foundation for modern grading and staging.

The unintended consequence of screening has been over-diagnosis – the detection of lesions that would never threaten survival

Even throughout most of the microscopy era, however, cancers were still first detected based on clinically apparent symptoms, and the microscopic insights were gained only after biopsy or surgery for a cancer that was usually already relatively advanced. In these decades, the pathologist largely confirmed and refined a diagnosis made – or at least suspected – by a clinician. With the advent of cancer screening in the middle of the 20th century, however, everything changed. Screening, by definition, entails looking for early cancer in otherwise healthy people. The widespread availability of Pap smears for cervical cancer (1950s), mammography and colonoscopy for breast and colon cancer (1960s) and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) testing for prostate cancer (1990s) allowed cancers to be diagnosed early, by biopsy: years or even decades before they would cause clinical problems. Over time – and without any particular intention or formal conversation – the fundamental diagnosis of cancer shifted gradually from a clinical determination by a surgeon or oncologist to a histologic determination by a pathologist, setting the stage for the rift we face today.

These years also marked the advent of the War on Cancer, and diagnosing a cancer meant treating that cancer. By the time I started training early in the millennium, screening had already saved millions of lives worldwide. However, the unintended consequence of screening has been over-diagnosis – the detection of lesions that would never cause symptoms or threaten survival if left undiscovered. As I entered practice, it was becoming clear that overdiag­nosis begets overtreatment and, even as screening saves lives, it harms many others through the side-effects, sometimes permanent and occasionally lethal, of unnecessary surgery, radiation and other treatments. Moreover, the diagnosis may also mean increased costs for life and health insurance, and remains associated with increased rates of depression and even suicide. So screening has proved highly controversial, driving vitriolic debates among healthcare researchers, particularly between generalists and specialists, and wild pendulum swings in screening recommendations and practices.

Cancer screening has evolved in concert with a revolution in molecular medicine. Our society’s massive investment in research over the past half-century has paid tremendous dividends. We now enjoy an unprecedented understanding of the process of carcinogenesis and of the spectacular complexity of the arms race happening every day – in William’s body, in mine, in yours, and in every animal’s – between the reproductive and evolutionary goals of individual cells and those of whole organisms. What we now understand about cancer’s origins, evolution and outcomes should drive a reconsideration of which individuals really need to bear the diagnosis.

The irregular clusters of cells we term ‘cancer’ based on their microscopic appearance are growing at all times in every body. To understand why the overwhelming majority of these are harmless, we need to return to the early history of life on Earth. Single-celled organisms emerged just about as soon as the planet became habitable, and for the next inconceivably long stretch of 2 billion years, these cells vied for survival and evolved innumerable strategies to outcompete – and sometimes consume – their neighbours and to adapt to new habitats. Eventually, evolutionary pressures drove some groups of cells to work closely together, until they started reproduc­ing as multicellular organisms; these newly specialised cells could contribute specific functions to the life of the organism and, critically, could no longer survive on their own.

Nearly two centuries ago, the cell theorist Matthias Schleiden observed that ‘each cell leads a double life: an independent one, pertaining to its own development alone, and another incidental, insofar as it has become an integral part of a [whole].’ This tension between independence and cooperation underlies all multicellular life – and explains a cell’s fragile pact with the body. A human being contains trillions of cells, each built around the same inherited DNA coding. These cells communicate constantly with each other – and with trillions more nonhuman bacterial and fungal cells that also comprise a healthy body – through myriad local and distant signals, regulating each other’s behaviour and growth, cooperating to maximise the reproductive success of the whole person.

And yet, every one of these cells carries the genetic memory of its single-celled past and its ancient imperative to replicate. In fact, each is kept in line only though a bewilderingly complex set of internal genetic controls and external interactions with other cells. Even after an adult stops growing, about 1 per cent of cells – billions – wear out and need to be replaced every day through cell division, requiring production of a complete and preferably perfect copy of the DNA.

I am stuck explaining cancer as we now understand it biologically to patients who still understand it culturally

Our DNA is continuously assaulted by radiation; environmental pollution; and inflammation driven by unhealthy diets, smoking, chronic stress and other factors. Furthermore, every time a cell divides, thousands of copying mistakes occur. Proofreading mechanisms correct the vast majority of these, yet errors do slip through. This imperfection is critical for a whole species, for without some rate of mutation, evolution would not be possible. For an individual, on the other hand, mistakes can be deadly. A relatively small number of uncorrected mutations can send a cell hurtling toward unfettered growth. This happens daily, in every animal.

The body monitors for such rogues; early identifi­cation and eradication of genetic uprisings is a fundamental job of William’s immune system. The arms race unfolds in every hour of every day: individual cells in some part of the body start to grow too quickly or in the wrong pattern, and immune cells identify and kill them. The odds are stacked against any one aberrant cell, but over the course of years, among billions of false starts, some mutations evade detection, take hold, and propagate. Most of these early events, however, do not define a clinically meaningful cancer in that they have no ability to cause symptoms or to spread.

Over time, some tumours acquire mutations that allow cellular growth to accelerate and others that impair error-checking. With enough regulatory signals removed, cells return to their primordial imperative to reproduce and spread. Evolution at micro-scale will favour those that can propagate fastest and travel farthest, no matter the cost to the organism as a whole. For breast gland cells, for example – whose one job is to sit in place and produce milk – to migrate into lymphatic and blood channels and thrive in the unfamiliar environments of bones or lungs requires many changes to their originally programmed behaviour. All along the way, the immune system will continue to contain, if not eradicate, incipient tumours. Only those rare exceptions that learn to grow indefinitely, travel and evade the immune system threaten the organism; these are the lesions that merit the historical and cultural terror carried by the word cancer.

Yet the huge scientific progress we have made has not translated in the public vernacular. As a physician, I am stuck explaining cancer as we now understand it biologically to patients who still understand it culturally. Biologic explication cannot fully supplant historical resonance, and translation goes only so far.

The process of carcinogenesis represents a molecular continuum. Cells acquire their first mutations without any visible changes under the microscope. Eventually, enough changes accumulate that a microscopically visible neoplasm (‘new growth’) emerges and, at some point after that, the neoplasm might acquire the capacity for meta­stasis. In some types of cancer, this happens frequently and very quickly; in others, it happens slowly, if at all. Critically, the appearance of a symptomatic or otherwise clinically detectable tumour may happen before or after the first cells metastasise – which is the reason screening is critical to identify potentially lethal cancers within the window of opportunity for cure.

William’s decision to undergo screening for prostate cancer, setting off the cascade that landed him in my office, is a perfect example. By the time a prostate cancer causes symptoms, it is nearly always too late to cure it, and dying of prostate cancer is both painful and protracted. Therefore, when PSA – a noninvasive blood test – hit the market in the 1990s, it was widely adopted. Diagnosis rates skyrocketed for prostate cancer, which for years has been by far the most common cancer diagnosed among men in the US and other countries. Many otherwise lethal cancers were found and cured, and prostate cancer mortality rates fell by half.

These findings are so common that the term ‘incidentaloma’ has joined the clinical vernacular

By the time of my residency training, however, there was little question that, for every death prevented through surgery and radiation, multiple non-threatening cases like William’s were detected through biopsy and were still treated aggressively. Of the many men thus overtreated, far too many suffered long-term side-effects. In part because of this problem of overdiagnosis, in 2012 the US Preventive Services Task Force recommended against any routine PSA-based screening. This recommendation had the intended effect of reducing prostate cancer overdiagnosis, but also drove an increase in mortality rates, particularly for Black men, reversing a 20-year decline. I met medical students who had been taught that PSA was the paragon of a bad screening test, and I began to see more men with incurable tumours who had never been offered one – or worse, had been refused a test even when they’d asked for it.

Grade group 1 prostate cancer – the lowest-grade form, with no immediate potential to spread or cause death – is exceedingly common. Among men who die in their 70s or 80s of non-cancer causes, these cells are found on autopsy in about half; among men in their 30s, the figure is about 20 per cent. They are not clinically meaningful cancers and may be better understood as a feature of normal male ageing. William’s low-grade prostate cancer was detected because he underwent an appropriate mid-life PSA screening, but it had likely been present for years before and was still many years away from threatening his life.

In addition to the many cancers detected through explicit screening, another large propor­tion are detected today more or less accidentally. I may order a CT scan for a patient with pain suggestive of a kidney stone, only to find that in addition to the stone there is an abnormality in the kidney, liver, pancreas or some other organ. These findings are so common that the originally tongue-in-cheek term ‘incidentaloma’ has worked its way into the clinical vernacular. Finding such lesions is occasionally fortuitous. I once took care of a young patient whose life was saved by an amoebic infection he picked up while travelling in South Asia; had he not been imaged for unrelenting abdominal pain, we likely would not have discovered his large, high-grade kidney cancer before it was too late. Much more often, however, we find and aggressively treat small lesions that would never have caused any problem if left undiagnosed, no matter their appearance under the microscope.

Public screening debates have grown bitter and tribal because both sides believe they are protecting patients from different versions of catastrophe. The surgeon, the oncologist and the advanced cancer patient see the metastases, the pain, the missed window, the death. The primary care physician or public policymaker sees the complications of treatment, the permanent declines in quality of life, the needless anxiety, and the costs. Both are reacting to real suffering, but the latter narratives more easily diffuse into intangible statistics, whereas the former resonate more powerfully and feel less forgivable. One patient asks: ‘Why did you talk me into the radiation that has left me with permanent bowel problems?’ while the other demands: ‘Why didn’t you order a simple test that could have saved me years of pain and let me watch my grandkids grow up?’

I regularly see both situations: patients suffering devastating side-effects of treatment they never needed, and others with incurable cancers that could have been found much earlier – some of whom had even asked for a screening test and were refused. My reservations about overdiagnosis and overtreatment have not made me a screening sceptic, but a screening test today should be only the first step on a possible journey to a diagnosis. William’s slightly elevated PSA should have prompted one of a dozen blood, urine or imaging tests designed to predict the presence or absence of potentially lethal prostate cancer. A negative test implies either a normal prostate or a grade group 1 cancer, and in either case we forego the biopsy – telling the patient more or less explicitly that if there is only low-grade disease present, both we and he are perfectly happy not knowing about it.

For the latter, the right path is active surveillance – deferring treatments and following carefully with every expectation of cure if there are signs of progression.

This paradigm was pioneered at my centre and a few others nearly 30 years ago, but has only recently gained traction in community practice, and implementation is still highly variable. In the US, too many financial, legal and cultural factors favour treatment over observation, a somewhat embarrassing reality to acknowledge in counselling visits.

We neither need nor want to know about every over-eager cell with the desire to grow but without the toolkit to travel

By the time William had his first visit with me, he had already been booked for surgery at one hospital and strongly pushed toward radiation at another. Many patients I meet in exactly this situation simply cannot get past the word, the diagnosis; they cannot reconcile with the idea that I would not want to treat what they see as a life-threatening diagnosis. Despite my best efforts at reassurance, none of my adjectives can tame the noun ‘cancer’, and too many patients wind up finding another doctor to offer unnecessary treatment.

Other examples abound. Basal cell carcinomas of the skin are so pervasive that cancer registries do not even track them. They can almost always be cured by simple excision. If neglected, they can grow quite large and can be disfiguring, but almost never spread, despite the carcinoma label.

Ductal carcinoma in situ of the breast by definition does not invade, and recent trials have suggested at least some such lesions can be monitored much like low-grade prostate cancer. In the case of thyroid cancer, pathologists have already crossed this bridge. A subset of lesions once classified as thyroid carcinoma were renamed ‘noninvasive follicular thyroid neoplasm with papillary-like nuclear features’ – mercifully abbreviated to NIFTP – because they don’t justify the full weight of ‘carcinoma’. Likewise, some small, low-grade bladder lesions once called cancer are now labelled ‘papillary urothelial neoplasms of low malignant potential’.

At the same time, we may be careening toward a new, fraught era of accelerated overdetection. All screening efforts to date have emerged from organ system-specific tests. Now, commercially available whole-body MRI scans marketed to the ‘worried well’ – and well-off – will surely multiply the number of incidentalomas we find every year. In parallel, so-called multi-cancer early detection tests promise to reveal molecular signals – fragments of DNA – of many cancers from a single blood draw. If they work well, they may save lives. But they also raise the stakes for the question that screening has already raised: when detection moves backward along the cancer journey from palpable lump, to abnormal cells, to molecular harbingers, what exactly are we naming? We neither need nor want to know about every slightly over-eager cell with the molecular desire to grow but without the genetic toolkit required to travel.

If the borders around ‘cancer’ are blurry, the boundaries of ‘normal’ are too. Normal-appearing cells often feature many cancer-typical mutations. Biology operates across bell curves, and clinical risk follows suit. In short, we don’t need to designate a given abnormality a cancer to justify treatment. We routinely remove colon polyps that may or may not presage cancer because the risks are typically negligible. In a more extreme example, some women with inherited BRCA mutations elect prophylactic mastectomy and oophorectomy – major surgery with substantial quality-of-life implications – because the spectre of possible future lethal cancer looms so darkly.

Medicine’s Greek and Latin shibboleths long served physicians better than patients. Dubbing a newly described but not-yet-understood region of the brain locus coeruleus lent an air of authority that ‘blue place’ would not have done. Today, our understanding of disease has grown along with our commitment to patient autonomy. But a very recent development in this vein, open medical records, exposes patients to language they may not understand. The result is that, all too often, the ‘you have cancer’ moment is lived only by a patient alone with a screen.

When I perform biopsies, I try to forewarn patients of the language they may see on the pathology report before we talk again, but there are limits to how much I can explain in advance. This problem is all the worse because we cancer specialists inhabit a borderland our vocabulary has not yet evolved to govern. The binary language of ‘normal’ vs ‘cancer’ suited the long epoch in which disease announced itself clinically but is badly strained in an era in which screening tests and incidental scans identify biological possibility long before clinical destiny. Pathologists describe what they see through the microscope, but a diagnosis is more than a description. When a word rises off a pathology report, whether into my exam room or the patient’s living room, it becomes prognosis, identity, fear, crisis.

Screening offers a transformative opportunity but can be implemented safely across populations only if we can distinguish and name ‘real’ cancers – those with the ability to spread and kill – as separate from the pretenders. Researchers and oncologists alike often speak of distinguishing ‘kittens’ from ‘lions’. Some kittens may evolve into lions, but these are the minority and can usually be identified before the lion escapes the enclosure.

We shouldn’t embark on a needless civil war against these minor malcontents

Modern medicine loves classification yet falls oddly short in oncology. Our international system for diagnostic coding recognises 18 codes in the heading of ‘contact with other nonvenomous reptiles’ yet only a single code for the huge spectrum of biology that is prostate cancer, regardless of aggressive­ness or clinical relevance. If we’re not careful naming the boundary between abnormality and disease, then we risk wounding our patients with the name ‘cancer’ itself.

In 2026, then, should my colleagues really have handed William a cancer diagnosis? Am I required to validate that diagnosis when everything we have learned over a quarter-century screams otherwise? Increasingly, we can tell the lions from the kittens. But after thousands of years, the karkinos still looms large in cultural memory, and the term ‘carcinoma’ on a pathology report still connotes pain, loss and death. I still meet patients who book appointments specifically to set up surgery and look at me with incredulity at the suggestion that that would be the wrong first step.

Perhaps it is high time for the medical community to reconsider how we define cancer, and to bring the diagnosis back into line with enduring public perception. Cancer, in the sense that has always haunted the public imagination, spreads and kills. Precursor lesions – molecular or pathological – are not ‘normal’, but we have no shortage of alternative vocabulary with which to label them, as well as the tools to safely follow them. Most will never amount to any meaningful insurgency, and we shouldn’t embark on a needless civil war against these minor malcontents. If we permanently address overdiagnosis by simply declining to diagnose low-grade lesions, we can screen much more broadly and with greater confidence. Such a change would improve trust between patients and their doctors, and between primary care providers and their consulting specialists. Relabelling would also very likely save thousands of lives.

William needs attention to his prostate no matter what labels we hang on it. He needs my counselling and monitoring. Someday, I may need to guide him toward treatment. But what he did not need, on the day he walked into my office having already rearranged his life around a word, was to live in the full shadow of a disease that was not yet threatening him. Revising the label would not only reduce overtreatment but would also finally realign our language with our science, with our systems of classification and with patients’ lived reality. Cancer is a cellular rebellion that spreads and kills. The rest of the microscopic borderland deserves a different, gentler name.

item.title: Affect theory
item.dc:creator: Aeon Video
item.description:
In the mid-1990s, thinkers pushed back against the idea we’re built by language, turning to feeling and the body instead

- by Aeon Video

Watch on Aeon
item.content:encoded: In the mid-1990s, some thinkers began to challenge the prevailing notion that our selves are largely constructed through language and turned to our bodies to make sense of how we build our worlds. In this video, the UK video essayist Lewis Waller examines what’s known as the ‘affective turn’ in the humanities. He traces how figures including the Canadian philosopher Brian Massumi and the US literary critic Eve Sedgwick looked to the embodied and visceral to help bridge Western philosophy’s mind-body divide and ‘think about ideas and matter at the same time’. A brief dive into a dense topic, this short nonetheless makes for a provocative exploration of the interplay of physicality, emotion and identity.

item.title: Paternity is poetical
item.dc:creator: Daniel Swift
item.description:
The notion that fatherhood and creativity are at odds is plain wrong, as both poetry and neuroscience are showing us

- by Daniel Swift

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

25 minute listen

Here’s an old story, often told. In Book 6 of the Iliad, Hector – dressed splendidly in bronze armour and a helmet with a horsehair crest – bids farewell to his wife Andromache. She begs him not to return to battle and hands him their newborn son. Hector raises the boy into the air, says a short prayer, and hands him back. ‘Go home, attend to your own handiwork / at loom and spindle,’ he commands, in Robert Fitzgerald’s translation: ‘As for the war, / that is for men.’

Hector is a father in the heroic mode, and his parenting style has long been irresistible to artists and writers. Few were shocked when the painter Paul Gauguin left his wife and five children in Denmark to pursue fame and art in Paris, then Tahiti. Such distance, they say, is good for a child. ‘The father, from his distance, supports, protects, nourishes his child,’ wrote D H Lawrence in 1922: ‘and it is ultimately on the remote but powerful father-love that the infant rests.’ Distance is equally necessary for the father who seeks to make art. ‘There is no more sombre enemy of good art than the pram in the hall,’ wrote Cyril Connolly in Enemies of Promise (1938).

This is a deeply self-serving story, of course. It’s nice for the male poet not to have to change diapers. But the argument that unsullied privacy is essential to creativity is tenacious. It surfaces when Virginia Woolf writes that ‘a woman must have money and a room of her own if she is to write fiction.’ Contemporary feminists have continued to respond to this archetype of generativity. In Jenny Offill’s novel Dept. of Speculation (2014), for example, the narrator vows never to marry but to become ‘an art monster instead’.

But what if domesticity – and specifically parenthood – is in fact generative for artists? What if the cliché of solitary male creativity got it wrong? We may begin with one nursing poet. In his poem ‘Frost at Midnight’, written in the winter of 1797, Samuel Taylor Coleridge pictures himself at home in his cottage on a frosty night. The owls cry outside and the frost rings the trees and he is alone, ‘save that at my side / My cradled infant slumbers peacefully.’ He addresses his infant son:

         Dear Babe, that sleepest cradled by my side,
Whose gentle breathings, heard in this deep calm,
Fill up the intersperséd vacancies
And momentary pauses of the thought!

He is transported to memories of his own childhood, and then his hopes for his son’s future.

‘Frost at Midnight’ is a poem about caring, in both senses of the word: caring for and caring about. As such, it is a surprising poem about domestic labour, which has invited comment from scholars. ‘What is truly radical about “Frost at Midnight” is Coleridge’s self-representation as a father in the traditional maternal posture of watching over a sleeping baby,’ notes Jonathan Bate. What Bate calls ‘the traditional maternal posture’ is what Hector calls ‘your own handiwork / at loom and spindle’. But perhaps it is not so radical to picture a poet who is equally involved in the work of parenting. Perhaps it is precisely fatherhood that made Coleridge a poet.

What makes ‘Frost at Midnight’ significant in Coleridge’s career is that it represents the crest of the much longer wave of his stylistic development. It is not just a great poem – it is the poem within which he becomes a great poet, and his growth as a poet can be tracked neatly against his experience of becoming a father.

Coleridge was far from home when his son was born. A lost revolutionary, he was always trying to save or at least improve the world, and he was preaching in Birmingham when word came by letter: Hartley, born to his wife Sara, on 19 September 1796. He met the news with shock and a trio of sonnets. ‘My o’erwhelmed Heart / Trembled, & vacant tears stream’d down my face,’ he wrote in the first of these. He sent this to a friend, and it was published only in 1847, after his death. He wrote another on the journey home, and here imagines that he might arrive to terrible news: ‘when I reach my door, / If heavy looks should tell me thou art dead …’ They are not charming poems, but repressed; so guarded even when apparently tender, as if he is trying out how he feels in the set form of an Italian sonnet. ‘When I saw it on its mother’s arm, / And hanging at her bosom,’ he confesses in the last of these sonnets: ‘Then I was thrill’d and melted.’ This is a cautious, half-convincing expression of fatherly love. A few days later, he wrote to a friend: ‘in truth, I have seen handsomer babies in my lifetime.’

‘Kubla Khan’, ‘Christabel’, ‘The Rime of the Ancient Mariner’ were all begun or completed within 18 months of his son’s birth

Because Coleridge narrated his moods, and wrote letters that turned into poems, he permits us to reconstruct a detailed timeline of his changing feelings towards his son. Later, it will be an unhappy story, and Hartley will live an unhappy life, but at first it did not seem to be going that way. By December 1796, Coleridge was planning to move his family to a thatched cottage in the village of Nether Stowey in Somerset. He wrote to a friend with enthusiasm: ‘I mean to work very hard as Cook, Butler, Scullion, Shoe-cleaner, occasional Nurse.’ He turned out to love nursing. By the start of February, he was writing to another friend: ‘You would smile to see my eye rolling up to the ceiling in a Lyric fury, and on my knee a Diaper pinned, to warm.’ This moment – of writing while nursing, of diapers and poetic inspiration – is the genesis of ‘Frost at Midnight’.

The creation of the father is also the creation of the poet. In the spring of 1797, Coleridge was writing 50 lines of blank verse a day. He began to develop his ‘conversation poems’, which drew from his letters to friends and family: their language is intimate, domestic; their topics often autobiographical. Towards the end of that year, he turned to what are now called his ‘mystery poems’, and are those for which he is most celebrated: ‘Kubla Khan’, ‘Christabel’, ‘The Rime of the Ancient Mariner’, all of which were begun or completed within 18 months of Hartley’s birth.

This was a moment of golden invention, and Coleridge knew that something had changed. Years later, in his rambling autobiography Biographia Literaria (1817), he recalled the transformation. ‘I retired to a cottage in Somersetshire,’ he wrote, and:

Here I found myself all afloat. Doubts rushed in … The fontal truths of natural religion and the books of Revelation alike contributed to the flood; and it was long ere my ark touched on an Ararat, and rested.

It is a biblical scene and a beautiful crisis, and suddenly all is both new and old.

‘Frost at Midnight’ was written over the winter of 1797 and completed by February 1798. It is highly structured. Coleridge’s biographer Richard Holmes calls it a ‘curve of memory and prophecy’, and, in four parts and carefully measured blank verse, it moves gently between the present moment, his own past and his hopes for the future. He thinks back to church bells – ‘the poor man’s only music’ – heard when he was a boy, and is filled with gladness that, while his own boyhood was spent in a great city, his sleeping son:

       shalt wander like a breeze
By lakes and sandy shores, beneath the crags
Of ancient mountain.

The poem ends with a blessing: ‘all seasons shall be sweet to thee.’

A man becomes a father and a poetic revolution follows. Not always, but often enough. Percy Shelley’s son William was born in January 1816. According to his biographer, also Richard Holmes, ‘after 1816: no other Romantic writer learned, and changed, and developed his art so swiftly.’ A century later, William Carlos Williams began what his biographer Paul Mariani describes as his ‘poem of initiation, his early crossing, his coming to some sort of terms at last with his own imperfect, vibrant world’ when his wife was pregnant. Their son was born in January 1914, and the poem was published that spring. Eighty per cent of the men who have won the Nobel Prize in Literature or the Pulitzer Prize for poetry were fathers. Celebrated philosophers, on the other hand, tend to be childless.

There are other ways to narrate poetic breakthroughs, of course. Coleridge’s development as a poet is often recounted – most powerfully by Adam Nicolson, in The Making of Poetry (2019) – as bound up with his friendship with Wordsworth, so that the two men together pioneered what we now think of as Romanticism. A pattern is not a recipe, and each of these examples has its own complications in the granular details. But the pattern is substantial enough – and counterintuitive enough – to be worth remarking upon. It is also supported by recent developments in neuroscience. As a field, neuroscience has been transformed by neuroimaging technologies: particularly functional MRIs, developed in the early 1990s, which permit researchers to track brain activity by measuring changes in blood flow. This has led to notable insights in two research fields: into creativity, and into fatherhood. Strikingly, the two may be linked.

Cognitive scientists distinguish between what are popularly known as Type-1 and Type-2 mental processes. The first are quick, unconscious, associative thoughts, while the second are slower, deliberate and conscious, mediated by the frontal lobe and executive control network. A 2020 study put EEG beanies on the heads of 32 jazz guitarists and asked them to improvise riffs while their brain activity was scanned. ‘Higher-quality improvisations were associated with predominantly posterior left-hemisphere activity,’ the study found, while ‘lower-quality improvisations were associated with right temporo-parietal and fronto-polar activity.’ This suggests that the creative process takes place – or takes place best – in the automatic and unconscious left posterior part of the brain, sometimes described as the ‘default’ system, rather than the more conscious, deliberative ‘control’ system.

The brain assists new fathers by encouraging the perception that fatherhood is meaningful

This feels like commonsense to anyone who has experienced states of creative ‘flow’, say. But it has specific consequences for our understanding of art as a process. Artistic creation is marked by activation of the medial prefrontal cortex and by deactivation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex. A 2015 study of 30 poets found similar patterns of activity. The poets at work showed increased activity in the inferior front gyrus, left middle temporal gyrus, and superior temporal sulcus as well as in ‘mesial temporal areas, including the parahippocampal gyrus, hippocampus, and amygdala bilaterally and subcortical areas in the left hemisphere.’ These are the areas associated not just with language, but with memory and improvisation. In a 2020 study, published in Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, expectant fathers who were played 30-second clips of infant cries interspersed with white noise responded to the infant cries ‘with increased activation in bilateral areas of the temporal lobe involved in processing speech sounds and social and emotional stimuli.’ Heightened activity within the temporal lobe is marked in both new fathers and poets.

While specific areas are activated at specific moments, it is key to see the brain as a network, and to trace patterns of connectivity between the regions. Both of these studies of creativity – of the guitarists, and of the poets – had a second step. The jazz guitarists were divided between experts and novices; and the poets, who were also compared by level of experience, were scanned twice, once while writing, then again while revising their poems. One characteristic of the experts is that they more effectively suspended the cognitive control mediated by the executive network; in the case of the revising poets, this was then re-engaged. The two processes are working together. David Rosen of Drexel University in Philadelphia, who led the study of the jazz guitarists, emphasises the importance of connectivity between the default and executive networks, which are both implicated in neuroscientific studies of creativity. He writes: ‘Increased connectivity across these networks may enable creative performance in a variety of domains, including music improvisation and creative writing.’

The clinical psychologist Darby Saxbe has surveyed recent developments in the scientific analysis of neurological – as well as hormonal and physical – changes in new fathers. In her book Dad Brain: The New Science of Fatherhood and How It Shapes Men’s Lives (2026), she points out that new fathers’ brains lose volume, for example, and this is chiefly in the cortex. ‘The cortex thinks ahead, makes sense of the world, and navigates our complex social lives,’ she explains. Meanwhile, the ‘cognitive and mentalising work’ that goes into fatherhood is indicated by the changing patterns of connectivity between different regions of the brain. Saxbe studies family relationships at the University of Southern California. Discussing a study by a junior researcher in her lab on how fathers experience a new sense of meaning, she notes that those fathers who reported an increased sense of purpose and meaning in their lives across the transition to fatherhood ‘had increased connections within the temporal poles, which are key components of the mentalising network, and the right hippocampus.’ This is pragmatic, Saxbe suggests: the brain assists new fathers by encouraging the perception that fatherhood is meaningful.

Such assistance can play out in surprising ways, and with surprising consequences. A study of the transition to fatherhood by Anthony G Vaccaro and colleagues at the University of Southern California, published in the journal Emotion in 2025, emphasises the impact of ‘resting-state connectivity between default mode and limbic networks’. It suggests that:

Functional connections between these networks may facilitate the integration of affective aspects of the environment with a sense of self and autobiographical memory, facilitating meaning-making throughout emotionally complex times.

This increased connectivity enhances the feeling of being closely attuned to the environment, and draws upon memories to help the self navigate and understand the present.

Again and again, the research points to intensified cerebral connectivity, and suggests that such changes take place regardless of biological relationship. A fascinating 2014 study conducted by Ruth Feldman and Eyal Abraham and their colleagues in Israel found the familiar patterns of response in homosexual male couples raising infants who had either been adopted or born through surrogacy. Summarising the study, Saxbe wrote that the homosexual fathers performing the primary caregiver role ‘showed amygdala activation similar to the primary caregiver moms and mentalising network activation similar to the secondary caregiver dads, as well as stronger connectivity between those two parts of the brain.’ The process of becoming a father – quite literally, thinking your way into it – is itself a creative act, driven by time, proximity and a sense of responsibility.

Neuroscientists tend to shy away from making direct and causal claims about the brain’s activity. They prefer the language of association, so that a brain region is described as being associated with certain habits or tendencies. That brain activity might lead to explicit changes in a poet’s style is necessarily speculative.

And yet: the shifting emphases and patterns described in neuroscientific studies of the brains of new fathers are echoed in the distinctive elements of Coleridge’s remade style: his assertion of autobiographical memory and its resonance in the present; his attention to his child and sense that his own identity is formed anew; his heightened creativity evident in what we might sentimentally see as a new openness. Perhaps we can use the neuroscience to read the poetry, and the poetry to read the neuroscience, in a kind of new longitudinal study, which returns us to the familiar poetic record and in it finds new forms.

Let’s take the example of confessional poetry, emerging as a group project in the late 1950s’ United States. The key characteristics of this new style – domestic details, departure from traditional poetic decorum – are shared by several poets, including W D Snodgrass and Sylvia Plath. In her essay ‘What Was Confessional Poetry?’ (1993), Diane Wood Middlebrook observes that the original four confessional poets were all recent parents of daughters when they had their poetic breakthroughs. She includes Robert Lowell and Anne Sexton as well as Snodgrass and Plath, but another candidate for the group is John Berryman, who was already a celebrated poet by March 1957, when his son Paul was born. Over the following 18 months, Berryman suffered, he said, from ‘an inability to stop writing verse’, and he remade his style and produced a great rush of the curious, brilliant poems later called his ‘Dream Songs’.

These poems are no longer in set, regular patterns. Harriet was born at the start of January 1957

Of the group, Robert Lowell is perhaps the purest example of a father poet – because of his enormous skill, and the drama of his life, and because the change in his own style is so stark. At first, Lowell wrote like this:

I saw the spiders marching through the air,
Swimming from tree to tree that mildewed day
        In latter August when the hay…

And like this:

When we were children our papas were stout
And colorless as seaweed or the floats
At anchor off New Bedford. We were shut
In gardens where our brassy sailor coats …

The two poems quoted here are taken from his collection Lord Weary’s Castle (1946), which was published when he was 29. Young Lowell loved rhyme. He later told an interviewer that he wrote his first poems unrhymed and then put the rhymes in after, like an obedient schoolboy doing his homework. Of the 42 poems in the collection, only one doesn’t rhyme completely and this has a complex system of repeated words at the line ends. Beneath the rhymes steps a cautious measure or rhythm. Try saying ‘I saw the spiders marching through the air’ aloud, or even tapping along: the 10 syllables and five balanced feet of iambic pentameter. Lowell followed this collection with a set of dramatic monologues in rhymed iambic pentameter, sometimes known as heroic couplets, published in 1951. He was taking form seriously.

Then, after the birth of his daughter Harriet in 1957, he wrote like this:

Given a year,
I walked on the roof of the West Street Jail, a short
enclosure like my school soccer court,
and saw the Hudson River once a day.

And like this, addressing his young daughter while shaving:

Dearest, I cannot loiter here
in lather like a polar bear.

These two poems are from Life Studies (1959). If they rhyme – and many don’t – it is in a sneaky, cat-like way. The line-lengths vary; these poems are no longer in set, regular patterns. Harriet was born at the start of January 1957. At the end of that year, Lowell sent a handful of new poems to his old friend William Carlos Williams with a note: ‘At forty I’ve written my first unmeasured verse.’

He offers the intimate details of a turbulent emotional life, all bound in elegant, beautiful poems that duck in and out of traditional poetic forms

Lowell knew that Life Studies was different. He explained to an acquaintance: ‘It’s all quite a different style, uses a lot of free verse, is intelligible to anyone on the surface, and heavily and directly autobiographical.’ This is a good definition of what soon became known as ‘confessional poetry’, arguably the dominant mode of US poetry of the second half of the 20th century, and which was first named in a review of Life Studies. Lowell’s volume won the National Book Award and has been celebrated ever since. Lowell himself saw the breakthrough in a humbler register. As he went on in his letter: it was only now, in ‘the years of my second marriage, and the birth of my daughter, that I have written to my mind what I really have had to say.’

What is wonderful about Lowell’s poetry from Life Studies on is the jumble of life and art. He offers the intimate, often tender, sometimes shocking details of a turbulent emotional life, all bound in elegant, beautiful poems that duck in and out of traditional poetic forms. A new set of materials alongside a new sense of poetic form: that mix is the characteristic of Lowell’s breakthrough. It is played out when he talks about his daughter and equally is the core of poems far removed from her.

For him, all had changed. ‘I’m really mad about my little daughter’ Lowell wrote to the poet Elizabeth Bishop, shortly after Harriet’s birth, ‘and feel as though I had been up to now lacking some prime faculty: eyesight, hearing, reason.’ He wrote to another poet, Adrienne Rich, in November 1960. This letter – from a poet to a poet – was filled with gossip about operas and writerly encouragement, but it is also a letter from one new parent to another, and to amuse her he breaks off: ‘interruption: Harriet has just come with her toy telephone.’ Harriet and her toys were for Lowell a brilliant, productive interruption: she prompted him to change his style. He now found himself, he went on, living in and writing from a ‘queer jumbled world’.

‘Parenting involves heightened emotional and cognitive demands,’ observes the study led by Vaccaro: ‘further emphasising the brain’s role in integrating diverse experiences into a coherent sense of purpose.’ Here is T S Eliot, who was not a father, defining the poet’s task in 1921: ‘When a poet’s mind is perfectly equipped for its work, it is constantly amalgamating disparate experience.’ The coincidence of language here points to an idea that we have often overlooked: that fatherhood and artistic creation are not antagonistic but congenial; that becoming a father might, quite simply, improve a new father’s poems.

But not only poems. Because poems are short and often time-stamped, they make legible the changing way a father may look upon and respond to the deep changes of fatherhood. The same forces are surely powerful, if harder to trace, in creative work by parents more widely, and echo across our cultural moment. We live, in the West, in an age of sensitive dads, dad jokes, and dad dancing: all signs of a cultural revaluation of fatherhood, freed from the stigma of patriarchy. The consequences are political as well as poetic. In The Argonauts (2015), Maggie Nelson powerfully describes the imaginative work and possibility of artistic freedom that come with parenthood, quoting the feminist thinker Susan Fraiman’s call for ‘the decline of the domestic as a separate, inherently female sphere and the vindication of domesticity as an ethic, an affect, an aesthetic, and a public.’ The poetry of fatherhood may take a thousand forms: the tender strangeness of Coleridge, the jumpy brightness of Lowell, the moving and original memoirs and novels by contemporary poets and writers including Ben Lerner and Jack Underwood as well as Nelson. But for each, the material entanglement of creativity and parenthood is a prompt, not a hindrance, to wild new work.

item.description:
Jürgen Habermas, the great defender of deliberative democracy, lived up to its demands: he never feared changing his mind

- by Emilie Prattico

Read on Aeon
item.content:encoded:
Listen to this essay

22 minute listen

Jürgen Habermas died on 14 March 2026, in the German town of Starnberg, aged 96. Every fall, from the mid-1990s into the late-2000s, he would come to Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois to teach and give talks, a visit that a dedicated group of students looked forward to every fall term. The year that has stayed with me is 2004, when he taught what he’d spelled out in Between Facts and Norms (1992), his opus applying his theory to democratic politics. Law, philosophy, history, political science: students spanned many disciplines to come watch the famous German scholar every week, dressed in Wrangler jeans and a tweed jacket, expose his theory of deliberative politics in his unmistakable nasal voice, thick German accent, and impeccable English. Max Weber and the Frankfurt School, which were intimate to him, since he’d been Theodor Adorno’s research assistant in the 1950s, came to life in his speech and then in schemas and figures in chalk as he theorised about them.

I understood almost none of it at first: words I’d read were coming to life in the room, spoken by their author, and still not resolving into sense. After several lectures, the shape came into focus: this wasn’t just Between Facts and Norms being rebuilt in public, but decades of work arriving at a single place. Since The Theory of Communicative Action (1981), Habermas had been arguing that reason survives in modern life only as something people do together, that is, by giving each other reasons and staying open to being moved by them, rather than by force, money or tradition. Between Facts and Norms was that idea turned toward law and democracy directly: a state counts as legitimate only when its laws could in principle be justified to everyone bound by them, through exactly that kind of open exchange. I’d watched that argument take root in a decades-long intellectual history. Thinking is a practice, it involves owing each other explanations, questions, answers. It is not a fast process, and doing it in public, out loud, in front of a room, is what makes it worthwhile.

I attended all of Habermas’s seminars during my time at Northwestern with great interest and, to be honest, a sense of awe. One day, the topic of the weekly seminar was inclusion, and I had argued, with the timid conviction of a green graduate student, that deliberative publics ought to be designed for inclusion, and that entry into these publics required that members accept the terms of deliberation themselves. ‘Well, we can tell that Ms Prattico really is a Catholic in the strict, universalist sense,’ was not the answer I expected – and what took me by surprise wasn’t that he’d made a joke of my religion, but that he’d seen me as a person with a history and a set of unexamined beliefs, something he’d noticed only by teaching me.

After the seminars, the class would sometimes go out for drinks. It was on one of these occasions that I understood where the joke had come from. I’d asked him what it had been like arriving in the US as a visiting professor for the first time, at the New School for Social Research in the autumn of 1967, which decades earlier had served as a refuge for scholars fleeing the same Germany in which he’d grown up. It was the start of a long habit of crossing the Atlantic: Princeton four years later, for the Gauss Lectures where he first tried out the turn toward language that would eventually become his theory of communicative action; then, decades on, Northwestern, where I got to sit in the room.

Habermas answered my question by going back further than any of that. He’d been raised Lutheran. Visiting the US in the 1960s and ’70s, he’d been introduced to the Quakers, and something in their small meetings had stayed with him, specifically the way they sought unity with everyone present. When he came to describe the conditions under which people could reason together as equals, he said he heard an echo of those meetings: conditions that hold only when everyone who could be affected by a norm isn’t just included but has a voice, can object, and speaks with sincerity. In those conditions, which go far beyond mere inclusion, the only constraint left on discourse is ‘the unforced force of the better argument’, as he put it in Justification and Application (1993). It didn’t feel like something he’d have said at the podium.

The Structural Transformation of the Public Sphere (1962), his seminal work originally published in German, made an argument about something concrete: 18th-century coffeehouses, salons and journals, where private citizens began treating the affairs of state as something they had standing to publicly discuss and judge, rather than simply obey. That habit, Habermas argued, was where modern democratic legitimacy first took root. The book also identified tendencies that would weaken it, too. He thought that the public sphere had already started to decay, folded back into spectacle by advertising and mass media, the public reduced from participants to an audience. It took almost 30 years for an English translation to appear. By the time it did, in 1989, Habermas had gotten a great deal of mileage out of the book in its original language; indeed, it had already made him a name outside Germany. When Craig Calhoun finally gathered the English-language response into a single volume, Habermas and the Public Sphere (1992), bringing together historians and theorists who challenged the argument, closing with a long response from Habermas himself, he could have easily spent the occasion defending a book that had already proved itself. Instead, he very openly contended with these critiques.

He came to think he’d been too sceptical about one piece of that story. But the warning itself never went away

Two critics stand out. Nancy Fraser argued that the public sphere was never actually open to everyone since it had excluded women and other groups from the start. She proposed replacing one public with many, arguing with each other, including publics formed by the very groups shut out of the first one. Geoff Eley made a related point from history: working-class and plebeian public spheres had existed alongside the bourgeois one all along, not before or after it. Both were extending an argument that Oskar Negt and Alexander Kluge had made back in 1972, that a whole proletarian public sphere existed, which Habermas’s book never accounted for.

Habermas answered these criticisms directly, in an essay called ‘Further Reflections on the Public Sphere’, printed as the closing chapter of Calhoun’s book. Habermas conceded that the exclusion of women was not incidental but built into how the bourgeois public sphere had worked from the start. Unlike the exclusion of underprivileged men, which was a problem of class, and in principle correctable, the exclusion of women, he now wrote, ‘has been constitutive for the political public sphere not merely in that the latter has been dominated by men as a matter of contingency but also in that its structure and relation to the private sphere has been determined in a gender-specific fashion.’ Habermas conceded that other public spheres had existed alongside the one he had taken as foundational. And he softened the warning, without abandoning it. He came to think he’d been too sceptical about one piece of that story, the early stirrings of consumer society. But the warning itself never went away. Sixty years on, he was still diagnosing a public sphere being distorted by commercial and structural forces, only now the culprit was platforms and algorithms rather than advertising and mass circulation.

He did not give up everything. He still wanted to keep the public sphere as something to measure democracies against, even if the history behind it was messier than he’d first made it look. The criticism and his answer to it sit in the same book, printed one after the other. Habermas’s views were open to being challenged, and open for us all to witness his thought in process.

Early in my dissertation work, I wanted to explore the role of experts in democracies through Habermas’s theory of deliberative politics, though I didn’t yet know how – I was, by any measure, stuck. My advisor, Cristina Lafont, one of his most trusted students, arranged a meeting anyway, at the hotel where he stayed during his visits to Northwestern’s campus in Evanston. He didn’t seem to mind that I arrived without a fully formed argument. Over almost two hours at what was then the Homestead Hotel, he had me lay out the problem as it stood, half-formed, and began working through it himself, out loud, testing it against his own theory as he went. He explained the three types of discourse that characterise deliberation – moral, ethical, and pragmatic – and was clear that when it comes to the moral, there are no experts: only individuals working out, together, what’s right in a given context.

Followed to its conclusion, that seemed to leave no room for expertise anywhere in deliberative politics. But he then turned to pragmatic discourse, where expertise does real work: finding the most empirically sound way to reach a goal already agreed on. Experts have no authority over what’s right, fair or worth valuing – only over facts. This was, in miniature, an argument he’d been making since his early work on science and politics: that treating value-laden political questions as though they were merely technical ones corrodes democracy. Decades later, in Justification and Application, he’d given the same worry he’d laid out in the trichotomy that morning sharper philosophical shape.

In later meetings in his office, more routine than that first one, I pushed the distinction further: what did it mean for climate change – a problem almost always treated, in his terms, as a matter of pragmatic discourse, all graphs and targets and carbon budgets, and almost never as a moral one. Who pays? What do we owe the people who pay? How should the resources that caused the damage be used? He didn’t have a ready answer. He asked question after question, testing the case against his own framework as though it genuinely hadn’t occurred to him before.

Justification answers only to the standards we happen to hold now: those standards can be shown wrong later

I’ll never know for sure if he was being generous or if I had shown him something he had not yet thought of in applying his own distinction. What stayed with me wasn’t the answer but the manner of it: a philosopher in his 70s, decades into a settled framework, still willing to test that framework against a case he hadn’t considered, in real time, out loud, in front of a student.

By 1999, Habermas gave up a position he’d held since 1973, the year he’d argued that truth is simply whatever people would agree on if they argued it out under fair-enough conditions. By the end of the century, he’d decided this was a mistake: it confused truth with justification. A claim can meet every test we have for it, survive every objection anyone raises, be about as justified as a claim can be, and still turn out false. That’s because justification answers only to the standards we happen to hold right now, and those standards can later be shown wrong. Truth doesn’t move when our standards do. Moral claims were different, he still thought: what’s right can only ever be what a fair conversation would settle on. There’s nothing else for rightness to answer to. But facts about the world answer to the world itself, not just to our best current agreement about it.

Several people had been pushing him toward this change. The US philosopher Richard Rorty pushed from the side from which Habermas was now backing away: for Rorty, there was no need for truth to answer to anything beyond what an audience could be talked into agreeing on, and he’d been making that case to Habermas for years. Lafont, my advisor, who’d arranged the hotel meeting, pushed from the other side, drawing on the US philosopher Hilary Putnam, who had spent much of his career arguing against exactly the kind of view that made truth depend entirely on human agreement. Lafont had argued since 1994 that Habermas’s own philosophical tradition, in its turn toward language, had drifted into a position where it couldn’t say the world holds firm no matter how we talk about it. When Habermas changed his mind, he moved toward Lafont’s position, not Rorty’s.

What Habermas never spelled out is what this does to moral and political claims once people stop being able to agree at all. Truth, on his revised view, still has somewhere to go even if everyone stops talking: the world doesn’t care whether anyone’s listening. His philosophy of Rightness never had that option. So, when the people who’d need to agree on something splinter into groups that no longer talk to each other, a factual claim can still be true or false regardless. A moral claim has nothing left holding it up, once nobody’s left in the room to agree on it.

Habermas gave up a position he’d held for almost 30 years because the people around him showed him it didn’t hold. He’d spent decades arguing that claims get redeemed when someone can compel you to answer, and then was compelled himself, and answered, in print, aged 70. Those critiques were not meant to be damning objections: they were precisely what his theory called for and was built on, ultimately.

Habermas returned to the subject in ‘Reflections and Hypotheses on a Further Structural Transformation of the Political Public Sphere’ (2022). His starting point is a particular relationship between beliefs and reality. Constitutional democracy runs on citizens holding certain assumptions about their own disagreements, namely that the disagreements are real, that they’re about something, that better reasons could in principle settle them. The system holds together only as long as those assumptions stay reasonably close to how politics actually works. His argument is that a public sphere, run through social media, threatens that relationship and widens that gap.

For Habermas, there are two forces at play in this widening. Platforms drop the editorial filtering that newspapers and broadcasters used to perform, and they turn every user into someone who publishes. For Habermas the deeper problem isn’t the resulting noise; it’s that heavy platform use produces something smaller than a public: semi-public spheres, self-enclosed, silos whose members can no longer perceive the wider public sphere as inclusive at all – claims to universality beyond their own horizon become, in his words, ‘suspect of hypocrisy’. That perception is itself the damage, on his account, as much as anything actually happening out in the general public sphere. He ends by insisting that ‘maintaining a media structure that ensures the inclusive character of the public sphere and the deliberative character of the formation of public opinion and political will is not a matter of political preference but a constitutional imperative.’

A factual claim still has to get the world right, whether or not anyone’s around to check it. Moral claims never did: they answer only to discourse. And discourse is exactly what he’s just described coming apart. He doesn’t draw the conclusion for moral and political claims himself, but it follows from putting his two books next to each other: the very thing a claim about what we owe each other had to answer to is the thing he says is disappearing, in an age dominated by exchanges on social media.

People retreat into whichever group agrees with them and lose their grip on a shared standard of true and false

Around that time, I reached out to my advisor for help asking Habermas for a foreword to a collection I was editing on Habermas and democracy. He was known for guarding his time closely – very few people had his email address, and he accepted only a handful of the hundreds of such requests he received each year. A couple of months later, an email came from an address I didn’t recognise: he had accepted, and written to say so himself. Amid the logistics, he added one condition: ‘You should send me at least a substantive part of the book before I can and would sit down and settle a few ideas.’ At 92, he wanted the material in hand before he’d commit to anything.

What came back was not a review of the interviews that make up the book one by one. He says so himself in the opening lines: it isn’t his task to comment on the conversations directly. Instead, he used the occasion to answer the standing objections to his view of deliberative democracy, and to close with the digital transformation that turned out to run through nearly every interview in the book – a theme he noticed himself, and named as central to the collection. One section was on experts, common sense, and the chain of translation that carries specialised knowledge into public reasoning: the same distinction he’d first sketched over a hotel breakfast, worked out now in far more detail, at the very end of his working life.

At one point, he writes that what’s been lost, in the democracies now regressing, is ‘a conflict of opinions that remains recognisable as a dispute about which position is backed by the better reasons.’ That’s as close as he ever came, in anything he wrote for me directly, to stating my own premise in his own words. He names the same loss again later in the foreword, describing people who retreat into whichever group already agrees with them and lose their grip not just on the public sphere’s inclusiveness but on the idea of a shared standard of true and false. What he doesn’t do here, any more than he did in 1999, is follow that loss when it concerns a moral claim once the discourse behind it comes apart. And that is what I tried to explore in my philosophical work since my dissertation.

He still believed the gap between expert and layperson could always, in principle, be closed by the right chain of translation. It was the one thing he never revised: he revised his theory of the public sphere, his theory of truth, but never the conviction that under the right conditions people can still reach each other. I am not persuaded that these conditions are as anywhere close to being met today – but that’s a disagreement I never got to have with him.

The remarkable engineering and tragic demise of the vessel that would end Britain’s dream to dominate the skies
